items.title: 14.4.4 Scalar Triple Product of Vectors in Terms of Components

blocks.text: Let \(\underline{u} = a_1\underline{i} + b_1\underline{j} + c_1\underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = a_2\underline{i} + b_2\underline{j} + c_2\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{w} = a_3\underline{i} + b_3\underline{j} + c_3\underline{k}\).

Now,
\[\underline{v}\times \underline{w} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the determinant formula for the cross product from 14.3: the \(\underline{i}\) term deletes the first column, the \(\underline{j}\) term (with a minus sign) the second, and the \(\underline{k}\) term the third.

\[\therefore\ \underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\]
\[= a_1(b_2c_3 - b_3c_2)\]
\[- b_1(a_2c_3 - a_3c_2)\]
\[+ c_1(a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds: the \(\underline{i}\)-component of \(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}\) is multiplied by \(a_1\), the \(\underline{j}\)-component by \(b_1\) and the \(\underline{k}\)-component by \(c_1\). The result is exactly the expansion of a \(3\times 3\) determinant along its first row, so

blocks.latex: \underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}
blocks.text_alt: u dot (v cross w) equals the determinant with rows a1 b1 c1, a2 b2 c2, a3 b3 c3

blocks.text: Which is called the determinant formula for scalar triple product of \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) in component form.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to use the formula: write the components of the three vectors as the three rows, in the same order as in \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\), and expand.
Two rules about determinants explain the properties of the triple product:
1. Interchanging two rows changes the sign. So swapping two vectors changes the sign: \([\underline{v}\ \underline{u}\ \underline{w}] = -[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\).
2. A cyclic change \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w} \to \underline{v}, \underline{w}, \underline{u}\) is two interchanges, so the sign does not change. This proves again that \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] = [\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}] = [\underline{w}\ \underline{u}\ \underline{v}]\).
Also, a determinant with two equal rows is \(0\) (used in 14.4.5).

blocks.title: Example 23
blocks.problem: Prove that dot and cross product are inter changeable in scalar triple product.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = a_1\underline{i} + b_1\underline{j} + c_1\underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = a_2\underline{i} + b_2\underline{j} + c_2\underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = a_3\underline{i} + b_3\underline{j} + c_3\underline{k}\), arbitrary vectors.
To prove: \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = (\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\).
Method: write the left side with the determinant formula, then rearrange the rows. Interchanging two rows of a determinant changes its sign, so two interchanges bring the sign back.

Step 1: Write the determinant formula
\[\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: this is the determinant formula just derived; its rows are \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) in order.

Step 2: Interchange \(R_1\) and \(R_2\)
\[= -\begin{vmatrix} a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: one interchange of rows multiplies a determinant by \(-1\), so we put a minus sign in front.

Step 3: Interchange \(R_1\) and \(R_3\)
\[= \begin{vmatrix} a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: a second interchange multiplies by \(-1\) again, and \((-1)(-1) = 1\), so the minus sign disappears.

Step 4: Read the new determinant as a triple product
\[= \underline{w}\cdot(\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\]
\[= (\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\]
Why: the rows are now \(\underline{w}\), \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), so by the determinant formula this is \(\underline{w}\cdot(\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\). The dot product is commutative (\(\underline{a}\cdot \underline{b} = \underline{b}\cdot \underline{a}\)), so it equals \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\).

Step 5: Conclusion
\[\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = (\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\]
Why: we started from the left side and reached the right side using only allowed steps. On the left the dot comes first and the cross second; on the right it is the other way round.
blocks.answer: \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = (\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\): the position of dot and cross can be interchanged in the scalar triple product.

blocks.title: Example 24
blocks.problem: Assuming \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) are unit vectors in a cartesian coordinate system. Prove that \(\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k} = \underline{j}\cdot \underline{k}\times \underline{i} = \underline{k}\cdot \underline{i}\times \underline{j}\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) are the unit vectors along the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) axes.
To prove: \(\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k} = \underline{j}\cdot \underline{k}\times \underline{i} = \underline{k}\cdot \underline{i}\times \underline{j}\).
Method: write each unit vector in component form and evaluate each scalar triple product with the determinant formula; show all three equal the same number.

Step 1: Write the unit vectors in component form
\[\underline{i} = \underline{i} + 0\underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\]
\[\underline{j} = 0\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\]
\[\underline{k} = 0\underline{i} + 0\underline{j} + \underline{k}\]
Why: the determinant formula needs the three components of each vector; a missing component is \(0\).

Step 2: Evaluate \(\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k}\)
\[\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(1 - 0) - 0(0 - 1) + 0(0 - 0)\]
\[= 1\]
Why: the rows are the components of \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\) in that order; we expand along the first row with signs \(+, -, +\).

Step 3: Evaluate \(\underline{j}\cdot \underline{k}\times \underline{i}\)
\[\underline{j}\cdot \underline{k}\times \underline{i} = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 0(0 - 0) - 1(0 - 1) + 0(0 - 0)\]
\[= 1\]
Why: now the rows are \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\), \(\underline{i}\). Only the middle element of the first row is non-zero, and its sign is minus: \(-1(0 - 1) = 1\).

Step 4: Evaluate \(\underline{k}\cdot \underline{i}\times \underline{j}\)
\[\underline{k}\cdot \underline{i}\times \underline{j} = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 0(0 - 0) - 0(0 - 1) + 1(1 - 0)\]
\[= 1\]
Why: the rows are \(\underline{k}\), \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\); only the last term survives.

Step 5: Conclusion
\[\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k} = \underline{j}\cdot \underline{k}\times \underline{i} = \underline{k}\cdot \underline{i}\times \underline{j} = 1\]
Why: all three values are \(1\).

Check: from 14.3, \(\underline{j}\times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k}\times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\), \(\underline{i}\times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\). So the products are \(\underline{i}\cdot \underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\cdot \underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\cdot \underline{k}\), each equal to \(1\). Geometrically this is the volume of the unit cube.

blocks.title: Example 25
blocks.problem: Find the volume of the parallelepiped determined by \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = \underline{i} - 7\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = \underline{i} - 7\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\).
To find: the volume of the parallelepiped with these three vectors as edges.
Method: the volume is the scalar triple product \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\times \underline{w}\) (14.4.2), and the determinant formula (14.4.4) computes it from the components.

Step 1: Set up the determinant
\[V = \underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\times \underline{w}\]
\[= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & -7 & -4 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: row 1 holds the components of \(\underline{u}\), row 2 of \(\underline{v}\), row 3 of \(\underline{w}\). Each sign goes with its number.

Step 2: First term (element \(1\), sign \(+\))
\[1\big[(-2)(-4) - (3)(-7)\big]\]
\[= 1(8 + 21) = 29\]
Why: delete row 1 and column 1; the \(2\times 2\) left over is \(\begin{vmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ -7 & -4 \end{vmatrix}\).

Step 3: Second term (element \(2\), sign \(-\))
\[-2\big[(1)(-4) - (3)(1)\big]\]
\[= -2(-4 - 3) = 14\]
Why: the middle element of the first row always takes a minus sign; minus times minus gives plus.

Step 4: Third term (element \(-1\), sign \(+\))
\[+(-1)\big[(1)(-7) - (-2)(1)\big]\]
\[= -1(-7 + 2) = 5\]
Why: delete row 1 and column 3; the \(2\times 2\) left over is \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -7 \end{vmatrix}\).

Step 5: Add the three terms
\[V = 29 + 14 + 5 = 48\]
Why: the determinant is the sum of the three terms. The result is positive, so it is the volume itself.

Check: \(\underline{v}\times \underline{w} = 29\underline{i} + 7\underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\) (cross product of \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\)). Then \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = (1)(29) + (2)(7) + (-1)(-5) = 29 + 14 + 5 = 48\). Same answer.
blocks.answer: Volume of the parallelepiped \(= 48\) cubic units.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In volume questions write the unit: cubic units. If the determinant comes out negative, the volume is its absolute value.

blocks.title: Example 26
blocks.problem: Find the volume of the tetrahedron whose vertices are \(A(2, 1, 8)\), \(B(3, 2, 9)\), \(C(2, 1, 4)\) and \(D(3, 3, 0)\).
steps:
Given: vertices \(A(2, 1, 8)\), \(B(3, 2, 9)\), \(C(2, 1, 4)\), \(D(3, 3, 0)\).
To find: the volume of the tetrahedron \(ABCD\).
Method: take the three edges from one vertex, \(\underline{AB}\), \(\underline{AC}\), \(\underline{AD}\), and use \(V = \frac{1}{6}[\underline{AB}\ \underline{AC}\ \underline{AD}]\) (14.4.3).

Step 1: Edge \(\underline{AB}\)
\[\underline{AB} = \underline{OB} - \underline{OA}\]
\[= (3-2)\underline{i} + (2-1)\underline{j} + (9-8)\underline{k}\]
\[= \underline{i} + \underline{j} + \underline{k}\]
Why: a vector from \(A\) to \(B\) is (position vector of \(B\)) \(-\) (position vector of \(A\)): subtract the coordinates of \(A\) from those of \(B\).

Step 2: Edge \(\underline{AC}\)
\[\underline{AC} = \underline{OC} - \underline{OA}\]
\[= (2-2)\underline{i} + (1-1)\underline{j} + (4-8)\underline{k}\]
\[= 0\underline{i} + 0\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\]
Why: same rule, end point minus starting point.

Step 3: Edge \(\underline{AD}\)
\[\underline{AD} = \underline{OD} - \underline{OA}\]
\[= (3-2)\underline{i} + (3-1)\underline{j} + (0-8)\underline{k}\]
\[= \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - 8\underline{k}\]
Why: same rule. All three edges start at \(A\), as the formula requires.

Step 4: Set up the formula
\[V = \dfrac{1}{6}[\underline{AB}\ \underline{AC}\ \underline{AD}]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{6}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & -8 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: the rows are the components of \(\underline{AB}\), \(\underline{AC}\), \(\underline{AD}\).

Check: \(\underline{AC}\times \underline{AD} = 8\underline{i} - 4\underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\), and \(\underline{AB}\cdot(\underline{AC}\times \underline{AD}) = 8 - 4 + 0 = 4\), so \(V = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\). The value is positive, so no sign needs to be dropped.
blocks.answer: Volume of the tetrahedron \(= \frac{2}{3}\) cubic units.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\): rows in the order \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w}\).
2. Swapping two rows (vectors) changes the sign; a cyclic change does not.
3. Dot and cross can be interchanged: \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = (\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\).
4. \(\underline{i}\cdot \underline{j}\times \underline{k} = 1\).
5. Parallelepiped: \(V = |[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]|\); tetrahedron \(ABCD\): \(V = \frac{1}{6}|[\underline{AB}\ \underline{AC}\ \underline{AD}]|\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the minus sign of the middle term when expanding.
2. Losing a negative sign inside a row, e.g. writing \(-7\) as \(7\).
3. In a tetrahedron question, putting the coordinates of the vertices into the determinant instead of the edge vectors \(\underline{AB}, \underline{AC}, \underline{AD}\).
4. Forgetting the factor \(\frac{1}{6}\) for a tetrahedron.
